summary: This document defines how to use Password-Based Message Authentication Code 1 (PBMAC1) from RFC 8018 inside PKCS #12 files, so more modern password-based key derivation functions can be used. It amends RFC 7292 and RFC 8018 and obsoletes RFC 9579.

plainLanguage.summary: A PKCS #12 file is a locked bag for keys. This lets the bag's seal use newer, tougher ways of turning a password into a lock.

questions: how does pbmac1 work in pkcs12
which key derivation function must pkcs12 support
subtitle: How PKCS #12 files can protect their integrity with PBMAC1 and modern password-based key derivation.

tldr.problem: PKCS #12 files protect their contents with a MAC whose key derivation function is specific to PKCS #12 and only lets you change the underlying message digest.
tldr.mechanism: The document lets the MacData structure use the PBMAC1 algorithm from RFC 8018, so PBKDF2 or scrypt can derive the MAC key. Implementations MUST support PBKDF2 with SHA-256 HMAC, and passwords are encoded as UTF-8.
tldr.outcome: PKCS #12 integrity protection can use more modern key derivation and meet regulations that allow only PBKDF2. This document obsoletes RFC 9579 and fixes its password encoding.

facts.label: Password encoding
facts.value: UTF-8, no NULL terminator or BOM

today: RFC 9879 is an Informational RFC published in September 2025. It obsoletes RFC 9579 and updates RFC 7292 and RFC 8018. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why PKCS #12 Needs PBMAC1
sections.content:
The PKCS #12 format from RFC 7292 is widely used to move certificates, keys and other secrets between machines, applications and browsers. Its integrity check relies on a password-based key derivation function that is specific to PKCS #12 and only allows the underlying message digest function to change.

This document, RFC 9879, amends RFC 7292 and RFC 8018 so the file can instead use PBMAC1, the Password-Based Message Authentication Code 1 defined in RFC 8018.

The RFC cites security concerns with the key derivation function from RFC 7292 and the much higher extensibility of PBMAC1. It allows PBKDF2 or scrypt to derive MAC keys and leaves room for future algorithms. It also helps in environments where PBKDF2 is the only allowed password-based key derivation function, because regulations differ.

The new syntax is designed so that legacy applications can still decrypt the key material, provided they can ignore failures in MAC verification. The authors amended PKCS #12 rather than adding an integrity field to PKCS #5, because the recommended way to protect keys needs both encryption and integrity protection.
sections.plainLanguage:
The old way of sealing the bag only let you pick a different glue. The new way lets you pick a whole different kind of seal.

Some rules say only certain lock-making recipes are allowed. Letting the file choose its recipe means more people can follow their rules. Old readers can still open the bag even if they cannot check the seal.

sections.title: Embedding PBMAC1 in the MacData Structure
sections.content:
The MacData structure in the PFX object is updated with four rules.

  • The id-PBMAC1 object identifier is a valid DigestAlgorithmIdentifier inside DigestInfo. If it is used, the parameters field MUST be present and consistent with PBMAC1-params.
  • The digest value MUST be the PBMAC1 result over the authSafe field.
  • The macSalt value MUST be ignored. For backwards compatibility it SHOULD NOT be empty.
  • The iterations value MUST be ignored. For backwards compatibility it SHOULD be a non-zero positive value.

The salt and iteration count that matter are the ones inside the PBMAC1 parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: The old spots on the form for salt and count are still there, so old readers do not get confused, but the new reader skips them and reads the new seal instructions instead.

sections.title: Recommended Parameters
sections.content:
For interoperability, every implementation MUST support PBKDF2 paired with SHA-256 HMAC, both for the integrity check and for the PBKDF2 pseudorandom function. Support for other SHA-2-based HMACs is RECOMMENDED. Implementations MAY use other hash functions such as the SHA-3 family, and other KDFs such as scrypt.

The length of the derived key MUST be written explicitly in the parameters and SHOULD equal the HMAC output size. For SHA-256 HMAC that means a 32-octet key. With PBKDF2, the keyLength field MUST be included in PBKDF2-params, and implementations MUST NOT accept PBKDF2 parameters that omit it.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone must know at least one common recipe so their bags open for each other. The recipe must also say how long the key is, so nobody can quietly make it tiny.

sections.title: Password Encoding and Deprecated Algorithms
sections.content:
Appendix B.1 of RFC 7292 notes that password encoding is underspecified. The older PKCS #12 MAC and PBES1 use a null-terminated BMPString. For PBMAC1, every password MUST be built from UTF-8 encoding, without a NULL terminator or Byte Order Mark.

This is the change from RFC 9579, which declared a BMPString; the text notes its test vectors already used UTF-8, and the change resolves an erratum.

On algorithms, attacks on SHA-1 HMACs are not considered practical, but implementations SHOULD NOT use PBKDF2 with SHA-1 HMAC. They MUST NOT use any message digest function with an output of 160 bits or less.
sections.plainLanguage: Everybody has to write the password down the same way, using the same alphabet, or the lock will not match. Old, weak recipes are discouraged.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Apart from the key derivation function, integrity protection is computed as before, so the security considerations of RFC 7292 and RFC 8018 apply.

KDFs generally have no lower limit on key size, so parameters could ask for a key of only 1 octet, which would ease brute-force attacks on the HMAC. The KDF parameters are not cryptographically protected, so implementations MAY refuse small key sizes or weak parameters. The RFC recommends rejecting any KDF parameters that give key lengths under 20 octets.

Attackers can edit unprotected KDF parameters, so a reader should check them rather than trust them.
sections.plainLanguage: If the key is only one tiny piece, a thief could guess it. So readers should refuse seals that ask for a too-short key.

sections.title: Test Vectors and IANA Registration
sections.content:
Appendix A gives six base64-encoded PKCS #12 test files, all using the password 1234. The first, with SHA-256 HMAC and PRF, MUST be readable by implementations. Two more valid files SHOULD be readable. Three invalid files cover an incorrect iteration count, an incorrect salt and a missing key length. Appendix B holds an ASN.1 module.

IANA registered the object identifier 76, id-pkcs12-pbmac1-2023, in the SMI Security for S/MIME Module Identifier registry, and updated the reference to this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC includes sample bags so builders can check that their readers work, including some broken ones that should be turned away.
